Parliament. Parliament is the legislative body of England and later the British Empire, with roots extending back to medieval assemblies and a modern history as the world's oldest continuously functioning representative legislature. Emerging from feudal councils of nobles, it evolved into a bicameral body incorporating commons and lords, eventually becoming the model for democratic institutions across the globe. The principle of parliamentary sovereignty—that Parliament holds supreme authority—became fundamental to democratic governance and the rule of law.

Parliament originated in the thirteenth century as assemblies of nobles summoned by the king to consent to taxation. The Magna Carta established the principle that even monarchs were subject to law. Over time, Parliament evolved to include representatives from towns and shires alongside nobility, gradually becoming the primary legislative body by the fourteenth century. It played a central role in the English Civil War, with Parliament's assertion of authority against royal absolutism directly triggering the conflict. Parliament emerged victorious from the Civil War, establishing the principle that Parliament, not the king, held ultimate power in England. It developed the concept of parliamentary sovereignty—the idea that Parliament represents the people and is the highest authority in the state.

Parliament became the model for democratic and representative institutions worldwide, influencing the American Revolution and republican movements globally. It developed a bicameral structure with the House of Commons representing commoners and the House of Lords representing nobility and clergy, each with distinct powers and prerogatives. Parliament evolved the tradition of ministerial responsibility, where the executive branch must retain the confidence and support of Parliament to govern. Its traditions of debate, precedent, and procedure set the template for legislative bodies from the United States Congress to the Canadian Parliament to Commonwealth legislatures worldwide.
